newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong sees no quick impact from telecoms pact.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong sees no quick impact from telecoms pact.

text.p: Hong Kong would see little immediate impact from a global telecoms pact reached at the World Trade Organisation (WTO), but the deal raised tantalising possibilities for the future, analysts said on Monday.
"The direct impact -- not much," said David Gibbons, regional telecoms analyst at HSBC James Capel. "Hong Kong's offer to the WTO merely embraced measures already in place or on track."
Officials from 68 countries agreed in Geneva over the weekend to open the global telecoms market to free market principles following three years of tortuous negotiations.
Hong Kong committed to open its market to call back and international simple resale of fax and data services.
The commitments will further erode the international monopoly of Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd, but their imminence had been known since last April.
"Hongkong Telecom is fully prepared for the liberation of the market in all these respects," the company said.
Call back is already in place, highly popular and growing by leaps and bounds.
Hongkong Telecom said late last year it had lost about 15 percent of International Direct Dial (IDD) traffic to call back, and rivals say it has lost more.
International simple resale (ISR) for fax and data has yet to get off the ground, but it should have a relatively minor impact, said Fredson Bowers, telecoms analyst at W.I. Carr.

While fax and data accounts for about 20 percent of Hong Kong's IDD traffic, which in turn accounts for about 60 percent of Hongkong Telecom's revenues, ISR will only apply to countries which have similarly committed to opening up.
Since half of Hongkong Telecom's traffic is with China, which is not a WTO member, only five or six percent of total IDD will be subject to cannibalisation by competitors, he said.
But Beijing is expected to join the WTO eventually, and that raises the possibility of foreign equity investment in China's giant and growing market, with Hong Kong firms in the lead, said Gibbons.
As part of the deal at the weekend, signatory nations will open up long-protected national monopolies and raise allowed levels of foreign investment.
China currently does not allow foreign investment in its telecoms service providers, but if it follows the global trend when it joins the WTO, Hong Kong firms could benefit.

"If that vast and explosively growing market opens up to much more significant participation from the rest of the world, then Hong Kong, as in most other forms of foreign investment (in China), would probably be a major conduit of that," he said.
Bowers said that while details were unclear, the deal raised the possibility the global accounting rates regime could fall under the WTO's most-favoured nation rules.
If that turns out to be true, then accounting rates, which determine what telecom providers pay each other to complete international calls, could fall to low levels very quickly.
Hongkong Telecom could benefit since its main destinations are North America and Europe, where accounting rates are low.
The company also said it would explore the substantial market access opportunities made possible by the deal.
It said it planned to apply for licences to provide virtual private network and internatinal simple resale services in the United States as well as in other countries.
